question: What is the main job of a mechanical ventilator when a patient cannot breathe well on their own?

options.A: To deliver oxygen and remove carbon dioxide
options.B: To keep the patient completely sedated
options.D: To cure the underlying lung disease

explanation: Think of the ventilator as a helpful partner. It steps in to help with gas exchange—bringing in fresh oxygen and blowing off waste carbon dioxide—until the lungs are strong enough to take over. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h1)

question: Why would a patient with a severe head injury and a dropping Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score be put on a ventilator?
explanation: When a patient's level of consciousness drops, they lose the reflex to keep their airway safe. A ventilator tube protects them from choking or swallowing saliva into their lungs. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h1)

question: In ventilator settings, what does the term PEEP stand for?
explanation: PEEP leaves a tiny bit of pressure in the lungs right at the end of a breath. This stops the tiny air sacs from collapsing like deflated balloons! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h2)

question: Which ventilator mode gives a full breath whenever the patient tries to inhale, while also making sure they get a minimum number of breaths per minute?
explanation: Assist-Control is like a supportive teammate. It senses when the patient wants to breathe and finishes the job for them, but it also has a backup timer just in case. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h2)

question: After putting in an endotracheal tube, what is the quickest and most reliable bedside check to confirm it is in the right place?
explanation: Carbon dioxide only comes out of the lungs! Finding CO2 right after the tube goes in proves it is sitting safely in the trachea and not accidentally down the esophagus. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h3)

question: A newly intubated patient is on a ventilator. You notice the left side of the chest is barely moving and you cannot hear breath sounds there. What likely happened?

options.A: The ventilator settings have too much positive end-expiratory pressure
options.B: The tube has slipped into the right mainstem bronchus
options.C: The oxygen source has become disconnected from the machine
options.D: The patient is developing a severe tension pneumothorax

explanation: The right breathing pipe (bronchus) is a straight shot down, so tubes often slide too far in and end up ventilating only the right lung, leaving the left side quiet. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h3)

question: Why can mechanical ventilation sometimes cause a patient's blood pressure to drop?

options.A: The ventilator directly causes vasodilation of peripheral arteries
options.B: Increased chest pressure reduces blood return to the heart
options.C: Sedative medications increase the heart rate too much
options.D: High oxygen levels make blood vessels constrict sharply

explanation: Pumping positive air pressure into the chest creates a tight squeeze around the heart's main blood vessels, making it a bit harder for blood to flow back to the heart temporarily. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is the recommended angle for lifting the head of the bed for a patient on a mechanical ventilator?
explanation: Keeping the bed raised between 30 and 45 degrees uses gravity to help stop spit or stomach juices from sliding down into the lungs. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h4)

question: What is the safest maximum time allowed for a single pass of suctioning an endotracheal tube?
explanation: When you suction, you are also sucking out the patient's air. Keep it brief (10–15 seconds) so they do not run out of oxygen or get a spike in heart rhythm. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h5)

question: When is the right time to suction a patient who is on a ventilator?

options.A: Every hour on the hour strictly
options.B: Only when clinical signs indicate retained secretions
options.D: Whenever the patient asks for it

explanation: Suctioning is rough on the airways and steals a bit of air. Always assess the patient first and only suction when you actually hear or see signs that they need it! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h5)

question: Which nursing care task is superstar at preventing ventilator-associated pneumonia?

options.A: Keeping the patient completely flat in bed
options.B: Administering high doses of intravenous steroids
options.D: Changing the ventilator tubing every shift

explanation: Keeping the mouth clean with chlorhexidine stops bad bacteria from throwing a party in the mouth and sliding down into the vulnerable lungs. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h6)

question: What directly causes barotrauma in a patient on a ventilator?

options.A: Lack of early physical therapy and leg movement
options.B: Inadequate hand hygiene by the nursing staff
options.C: Bacterial infection growing in the endotracheal tube
options.D: High airway pressure or excessive lung volume

explanation: Too much pressure or blowing the lungs up like an over-inflated balloon can pop delicate air sacs, causing air to leak where it shouldn't. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h6)

question: What is the main point of doing a Spontaneous Breathing Trial (SBT)?

options.A: To measure the exact size of the patient's lung capacity
options.B: To clean out thick secretions from the lower airways
options.C: To give the mechanical ventilator a chance to rest and cool down
options.D: To test if the patient can breathe without full ventilator support

explanation: An SBT dials back the machine's help to see if the patient's own breathing muscles are ready to take over the job. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h7)

question: During a breathing trial, your patient starts sweating heavily, using their neck muscles to breathe, and their heart rate shoots from 85 to 130 beats per minute. What should you do?

options.A: Stop the trial and resume previous ventilator support settings
options.B: Encourage the patient to keep trying because anxiety is normal
options.C: Administer a strong sedative medication to calm the patient down
options.D: Remove the endotracheal tube immediately to finish extubation

explanation: Whoops, they are struggling! These are red flags that the breathing trial is failing. Put the ventilator settings right back where they were and let the machine help them rest. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h7)

question: Why should you still talk and explain procedures to a sedated patient on a ventilator?

options.A: It satisfies the legal requirement for written informed consent
options.B: It helps the mechanical ventilator synchronize with the patient's heart
options.C: Unconscious or sedated patients may still perceive and process sound
options.D: Hospital regulations require talking to every patient on a machine

explanation: Hearing is often the last sense to go. Explaining what you are doing is a kind, human act that helps soothe fear and confusion. [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h8)

question: What is the best way to help an awake, intubated patient communicate with you?

options.A: Using communication boards or writing tablets
options.B: Asking the patient to whisper loudly around the tube
options.C: Relying entirely on family members to translate lip movements
options.D: Temporarily deflating the cuff on the tube so they can talk

explanation: Because the breathing tube sits right through the vocal cords, speaking is impossible. Simple writing pads or picture boards are a nurse's best friend here! [learn more](GNS321_U2_T10#GNS321_U2_T10_h8)
